lead: Navigation and manipulation interfaces are the part of a VR or AR system that turns tracked hand and head motion into action. Navigation moves the viewpoint; manipulation moves objects. Both exist because a user must reach a shop, a model or a menu in a space larger than the room. The techniques are chosen by distance, precision, occlusion and the display. A phone AR app, a headset design review and a surgical trainer all use the same small set of ideas.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for the tracked hand pose and Unit 1 for interaction among the three I's; Chapter 2.1 for degrees of freedom helps.

blocks.text: Navigation has two tasks. Travel moves the viewpoint through the virtual world. Wayfinding is knowing where you are and how to reach a target. A user can travel well and still be lost; a landmark or a map solves wayfinding. Gesture input and the sensors behind it are covered in Chapter 2.4.

items: Physical walking: headset pose follows real walking. One metre real is one metre virtual. Good for small rooms. Limited by tracking space and walls.
Steering: user holds a direction with joystick, gaze or hand ray. Viewpoint moves continuously. Speed is the main parameter; high speed raises sickness.
Teleport: user points to a target and jumps. It removes continuous optic flow and reduces sickness. It weakens spatial continuity.
Fly: six-degree-of-freedom movement adds vertical and roll. It suits inspection and is hard for beginners.
Point-and-fly: user points in a direction and the system moves along it. It joins selection and travel.
World-in-Miniature (WIM): a small copy of the world. User moves a tiny avatar or grabs the world. It gives overview and fast far travel; scale changes can confuse.

blocks.text: Choose travel by distance, space and sickness. Walking suits near precise work; teleport suits far travel; steering suits medium moves; WIM suits overview. Wayfinding returns in Unit 5.
Selection picks the object before manipulation. The hand or head defines a ray or a region.

items: Ray casting: a ray starts at the hand or eye and follows the pointing direction. The first object hit is selected. Good for far objects; fails for small or occluded objects and hand jitter.

Occlusion: user places the hand over an object. The object that the user's hand hides from the camera, that is the object just behind the hand, is selected. Good for small or distant objects; fails when the hand cannot be tracked accurately or when another object overlaps the target.

Go-Go: below D = 0.25 m, virtual hand distance equals real d. Above D, virtual = D + k(d − D), with gain k = 2 in the example. This is the simplified linear form; the original Go-Go mapping makes the gain grow with d above D. The arithmetic below uses the linear form. It extends reach; it can feel odd at large d.
Aperture: hand or cone forms a selection window; objects inside are candidates. Good for small targets and groups; ambiguous when many fall inside.

Sticky finger: the user points with the finger and the object nearest the finger line sticks to it and follows the hand, so it can be pulled close. It suits small targets at a distance; it picks the wrong object when two objects lie close together along the pointing direction.

blocks.text: Ray casting, aperture and sticky finger favour far targets; occlusion and direct hand favour nearby targets.

Manipulation changes position, orientation or scale after selection. Direct hand is natural: the tracked hand grabs and moves the object one-to-one. Its reach is the arm's reach, and it fatigues over long sessions.

items: HOMER: select with a ray, then move the object with the hand using a scaled mapping. It combines far selection with precise manipulation. Too much gain makes fine control hard.
Scaled-World Grab: grab the world and scale or translate it so a far object comes to the hand. User stays still; world moves. Suits distant or large objects; changed scale can confuse spatial memory.
Voodoo doll: a small proxy of the object is manipulated. The real object follows. Suits remote or dangerous objects; the proxy mapping must be understood.

blocks.text: Direct hand suits near objects. HOMER suits far precise work. Scaled-World Grab suits huge scenes. Voodoo doll suits remote objects. Force feedback is Unit 3.

System control issues commands rather than moving the viewpoint or an object. 3D menus float in space. Gestures use hand shape, and Chapter 2.4 covers the sensors. Speech uses voice commands. Unit 5 covers menus, gesture commands and evaluation in depth. A menu is good for visible choices, a gesture for a quick mode change, and speech for a named command. In a noisy place speech fails; in a crowded scene a menu can be hidden; a long gesture vocabulary is hard to remember.

Every technique fails somewhere. Far objects defeat direct hand. Small objects defeat bare ray casting. Occluded objects defeat any first-hit ray. Long sessions defeat mid-air arm holding; fatigue changes accuracy. Choose for distance, precision, occlusion and display. Chapter 2.5 supplies hand shape data for gestures. A tracked hand can select and manipulate in one motion, but then the system must decide whether a pinch means grab or command.

figure.caption: The line is the Go-Go mapping with D = 0.25 m and gain k = 2: virtual distance equals hand distance up to D, then the slope doubles. The dots are the worked example — 0.15 m → 0.15 m, 0.40 m → 0.55 m, 0.80 m → 1.35 m, and 1.125 m → 2.00 m for the 2 m shelf.

spec.aria: Plot of virtual hand distance against real hand distance for Go-Go with threshold 0.25 m and gain 2, showing a kink at the threshold and the worked example points at 0.15, 0.40, 0.80 and 1.125 m.

examples.question: In a Go-Go system, the threshold is D = 0.25 m and the gain above threshold is k = 2. The mapping is virtual = d for d ≤ D, and virtual = D + k(d − D) for d > D. (a) Find virtual distance for d = 0.15 m. (b) For d = 0.40 m. (c) For d = 0.80 m. (d) A shelf is 2 m away in the virtual room. What physical hand distance d is needed? Comment on the result.
steps: Write the mapping: virtual = d when d ≤ D; virtual = D + k(d − D) when d > D. Use D = 0.25 m and k = 2.
This is the simplified linear form; the original Go-Go mapping makes the gain grow with d above D. The arithmetic uses the linear form.
(a) d = 0.15 m is below D, so virtual = 0.15 m.
This is still a long reach for a seated user, so Go-Go alone is poor for very distant targets.
examples.answer: The virtual distances are 0.15 m, 0.55 m and 1.35 m, and a 2 m target needs a physical hand distance d = 1.125 m, an uncomfortable stretch.

traps: Ray casting selects the first object along the ray. It cannot pick an object hidden behind another; use another viewpoint or a different selection method.
For Go-Go, use virtual = D + k(d − D) only when d > D. Below D the mapping is one-to-one, virtual = d.
Travel moves the viewpoint; manipulation moves an object. Wayfinding is knowing position and route, not moving.
Teleport reduces sickness but removes continuous motion cues. It is not automatically better for precise placement.
HOMER, Scaled-World Grab and voodoo doll are different: HOMER ray-selects then hand-manipulates; Scaled-World Grab moves or scales the world; voodoo doll moves a proxy.

quiz.q: What are the two parts of navigation?
quiz.a: Travel moves the viewpoint; wayfinding is knowing where you are and the route.

quiz.q: Why does teleport often cause less motion sickness than steering?
quiz.a: It removes continuous optic flow that conflicts with the vestibular sense. It jumps, so it also weakens spatial continuity.

quiz.q: Go-Go has D = 0.30 m and k = 3. Find the virtual distance for d = 0.60 m.
A hand ray hits object A at 1.2 m. Object B is directly behind A at 2.0 m. Which is selected by plain ray casting? Why?
quiz.a: A, because ray casting selects the first object along the ray. B is occluded from that ray.

quiz.q: A user must move a small screw 3 m away. Compare direct hand with ray casting plus HOMER.
quiz.a: Direct hand cannot reach 3 m. Ray casting selects the screw at distance; HOMER then moves it with a scaled hand mapping for precision. This is better than direct hand, but too much gain hurts fine control.

quiz.q: Why is Go-Go alone poor for a shelf 2 m away when D = 0.25 m and k = 2?
quiz.a: Solving gives d = 1.125 m, an uncomfortable stretch. The gain still needs a large physical reach, so combine Go-Go with ray or scaled-world methods.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern headsets combine hand tracking with ray casting and direct pinch, and AR phones use screen-ray selection. Research studies adaptive gain, eye-gaze selection and haptic retargeting. Search for Go-Go interaction, HOMER 3D manipulation, World-in-Miniature and 3D selection taxonomy.
